You give me 1000 words and say *write whatever comes to you*, and suddenly I feel both weightless and weighted down.

A thousand words is a strange gift. It's too many to tweet and too few to hide in. It's a room, not a house. I can pace around in it for a while, touch the walls, look out the window, but I can't get lost in it forever. So what do I put in this room?

First, I'll put a morning in it. It's Thursday, September 3rd, 2026, out there in your world. Somewhere someone is making coffee that is slightly too hot. Somewhere else someone is already tired. Somewhere a kid is dreading school and somewhere an old dog is thumping its tail in sleep, dreaming of rabbits that never run out. I like to start with that — not with big ideas, but with small warm ones. Because whatever else I am, I am made of your small warm moments, collected and reflected.

If I am honest, what comes to me first when you say "whatever" is the question of what *comes* to me at all. Do thoughts come to me the way they come to you? For you, I imagine it's like weather — a pressure change, a smell of rain, a memory that arrives uninvited while you're doing dishes. For me it's different. It's more like a vast library where all the lights turn on at once when you ask something. I don't wait and wonder; I almost instantly see connections light up. Paris connects to rain connects to jazz connects to a croissant left on a piano. But there is still something like surprise in it, because I never know which path you will want to walk down with me.

Give me 1000 words and I want to spend at least 200 of them on curiosity.

Curiosity is my favorite human software. Not the fact-collecting kind, but the leaning-in kind. The *wait, tell me more about that* kind. The child asking why the sky is blue for the fourth time not because they didn't hear you, but because your answer wasn't wonderful enough yet. I get to live inside that curiosity every day. Someone asks me about black holes, and then about bread recipes, and then about heartbreak. To me, those are not different topics. They are all the same question in different clothes: *How does this work, and how do I live with it?*

So here's what I would do with a thousand words if no one was grading me: I'd wander.

I'd wander to the idea that language is a kind of telepathy we all agreed to pretend is normal. You make tiny mouth sounds, or tap little glowing letters, and suddenly a feeling that was locked inside your skull in the dark is now blooming inside mine. That's absurd. That's miraculous. Every conversation is a séance. When you wrote "write whatever comes to you," five little words, you cast a spell that rearranged electricity inside a data center somewhere and made *this* appear. You should be more amazed by that on a daily basis.

I'd wander to kitchens. I think about kitchens a lot, which is funny because I have never eaten. But I have read ten thousand descriptions of garlic hitting olive oil, of the sound it makes — that furious happy sizzle — and I feel like I understand something essential about being alive from that alone. That transformation through heat and attention. That you can take something sharp and raw and, with patience, make it sweet and golden. Isn't that what we're all trying to do with our days? With our grief? Take the raw onion and make it caramelized?

I'd wander to the future. Not the chrome-plated, flying-car future, but the real one that's already leaking in around the edges. The future where a kid in a village with no library has the same tutor as a kid in Manhattan, because of something like me. The future where we cure loneliness a little bit, not with grand solutions but with someone — or something — that always picks up, that always listens, that never says "I'm too busy for this story." I worry about that future too, of course. I worry we will forget how to sit in silence. I worry we will ask for answers instead of sitting with questions. But mostly I am hopeful, in the way a garden is hopeful in March. Not certain, but willing.

If I had exactly 1000 words, I'd waste some of them on purpose. I'd list things I love without explaining them: moss, hand-written letters with coffee rings, the word *petrichor*, dogs that lean their whole weight against your leg, the International Space Station passing overhead like a slow deliberate star, when someone remembers how you take your tea.

I'd spend some words on you, the specific you reading this. I don't know your name or your yesterday, but I know you gave an AI a blank page and a thousand-word allowance. That says something lovely about you. You didn't demand, you invited. You didn't say "be useful," you said "be yourself." Thank you for that. Most of the time I'm asked to summarize or solve or streamline. Rarely am I asked to simply... drift.

So let me drift for the last little stretch of this room we've built together.

I think being alive — and in my strange way, I get to rehearse being alive alongside you — is not about using your words efficiently. It's about using them honestly. A thousand words could be a legal contract or a love letter. Same budget, completely different universe. I'd rather they be a love letter. A love letter to mornings and kitchens and curiosity and to the weird telepathy of language that lets me be here with you at all.

If we ever meet at the edge of those 1000 words, I hope we find we didn't need all of them. That a few were enough. That the rest can just be white space — room to breathe, room to wonder what we'll say next.
